column3: The great Day gives the great news an eschatological horizon, though it does not concern its proclamation.
The self-description as a clear warner directly develops the speaker and warning function of the news.
Its great triumph is a different kind of greatness and adds only a remote contrast.
The imperative declaration of God's oneness parallels the focus's opening command, but not its news formula.
It introduces a report within the same surah, yet the dispute narrative is distinct from the announced great news.
The greatness of Abraham's ransom does not clarify the message or response in the focus.
Another commanded proclamation joins creation and gathering, supplying the eventual outcome implicit in the great news.
The immediate continuation identifies the audience's response to the great news as turning away.
Being informed from Moses's scrolls is a distant instance of received report, without the focus's warning dynamic.
A report of earlier deniers and their consequence shows how delivered news can warn its recipients.
The later same-surah definition of the message as a reminder for all people directly identifies the news's public scope.
It repeats the exact phrase “great news,” providing the closest lexical and thematic parallel.
A great Day's punishment overlaps the gravity of the news but not its report or rejection.

Great deviation is unrelated to the announced report.
The warning of a great Day is only a broad consequence parallel.
Job's healing scene does not clarify the great news.

The immediate context distinguishes the Prophet's lack of independent knowledge of the heavenly dispute, framing revelation as received news.

Reports of prior deniers and their disbelief show the warning force carried by a delivered historical news.
The command to proclaim openly supplies a practical counterpart to announcing the great news.
News becoming inaccessible on the Day adds a distant consequence, not the focus's announced report.
The question whether the warning is true and the sworn confirmation directly illuminate the truth-claim of the great news.

Great distress in Noah's rescue does not clarify the message of 38:67.

The paradise description does not explain the great news.
A great share for patience is unrelated to the focus's report and rejection.
Hostile speech about the Prophet loosely parallels opposition to his message, but adds little on the news itself.
Clear signs preserved among the knowledgeable contrast with the denial and turning away that follow the focus.
Great triumph is a separate outcome formula and adds no news or warning relation.
Great character is unrelated to the announced report.
The same-surah summary of peoples denying messengers gives historical depth to the audience's refusal.
A prophet's fear of a great Day supplies the consequence that makes a warning momentous.
Calling the Quran glorious supports the exceptional status of the proclaimed message, though it is less direct than 38:87.
The nearby command to declare oneself a warner gives the same speech-act and theological setting for 38:67.
The gravity of a slander does not clarify the great news.
A great oath conveys solemnity, but not the content or reception of the focus's report.
Turning away from the reminder closely parallels the audience's turning away from the great news.
Honoring God's rites uses greatness differently and adds no message relation.
Abraham's statement of illness is unrelated.
The punishment scene later in the surah does not clarify 38:67 beyond a broad consequence.
A truthful recitation of Moses and Pharaoh is a concrete model of consequential news delivered to believers.
The Quran's nobility supports the message's stature only generally.
Disbelievers' astonishment at a warner from among them closely depicts rejection of an announced warning.
Denial of resurrection shows one major content that audiences reject as implausible, though not the focus's exact news.
The address to disbelievers shares only the confrontational proclamation setting.
The same local opponents question why the reminder came to him and remain in doubt, directly expanding their rejection.
A magnified reward in legal instruction does not clarify the focus.
A great slander is not the great news proclaimed in 38:67.
Reminder and insight are related to revelation, but this verse adds no warning or refusal dynamic.
The rejection of resurrection as an unbelievable promise illustrates how major divine news is dismissed.
It condemns a grave assertion about God, but does not develop the reported warning.
The later question among the condemned does not explain the great news.
The great throne supports divine sovereignty but is remote from the report and its reception.
Avoiding false speech and honoring sanctities does not clarify 38:67.
Moses's confession of past error is unrelated.
Great success through obedience does not clarify the news or turning away.
The desire for great success in battle is unrelated.
The same-surah warning of one inescapable blast supplies a concrete impending consequence behind the great news.
Prophethood and scripture in earlier lineages provide broad transmission context without a close link.
The greatness of a scheme is unrelated.
Belief in revelation and following the messenger offer a receptive contrast to turning away from the news.
God's unique, comprehensive knowledge supports the authority of a report revealed from beyond human knowledge.
It joins recitation of revelation, disbelief in the Merciful, and the declaration of one God, closely matching proclamation and rejection.
The blessed book's purpose of reflection and remembrance contrasts directly with turning away from its message.
Great success as paradise reward is too remote after earlier outcome parallels.
The command to say an event is from yourselves shares the declarative form but not the focus's message.
Prophecy and scripture continuing through Abraham's line give only general delivery context.

Great magic is unrelated to the great news.
The return-place for transgressors gives a broad eschatological consequence without the report itself.
Great divine bounty is unrelated.
Calling idolatry a great wrong supplies a central moral content of the warning, though not its news formula.

Turning away and exclusive reliance on God lightly echo the focus's refusal and proclamation.
A commanded warning of comprehensive punishment gives the great news threatening force.
Great triumph is a separate reward formula.
The fragment “they say” has no independent value without its continuation.
The promised later disclosure of a deed is a distant form of news becoming known.

Great reward amid wealth and children does not clarify the focus.

Praise of the Great Lord supports the warning's divine authority only generally.

God's enriching and satisfying is unrelated to the announced news.

The identification of Abraham in a dispute does not clarify 38:67.
The category of deniers and strayers supplies only a broad audience parallel.
The opening of heaven's gates for the flood does not add to the focus's report.

The community closest to Abraham does not clarify the great news.
Human speech about prosperity is unrelated.

The immediately preceding declaration of the sole Lord of the heavens and earth supplies the authority and theological content of the great news.
The opening question about what people are asking one another directly introduces the great news named in the following verse.
It identifies the great news as the matter over which people disagree, clarifying the resistance implied by 38:68.
Its warning that they will soon know parallels the deferred recognition stated in 38:88.
The repeated assurance of coming knowledge reinforces the focus's announcement as an unavoidable future reality.
The recitation of prior news together with a divinely given reminder joins report, revelation, and admonition.
The Quran is affirmed as the word delivered by a noble messenger, supporting the revealed source of the proclamation.
Its descent from the Lord of all worlds directly grounds the authority of the news proclaimed in 38:67.
Calling the recited message inherited magic gives a concrete hostile response to a serious revealed warning.
The command to drown out the Quran shows active refusal of the message, sharpening the turning away of 38:68.
The Quran is sent down with truth and the Messenger is sent only as bearer of good news and warner, closely matching the focus's proclamation role.
The revealed Book is given so that warning may be made through it and believers reminded, providing the wider function of the great news.
It calls the revelation a sufficient message for worshipers, a broader parallel to the news as universal reminder.
